newsitem.title: USA: GM sees no immediate U.S. impact from strike.
newsitem.headline: GM sees no immediate U.S. impact from strike.

text.p: General Motors Corp. said Friday the strike at its Canadian operations has not yet affected its U.S. factories, which are scheduled to resume normal production on Monday.

"At the present time, it appears that it is not going to have an immediate effect," GM spokesman Gerry Holmes said of the walkout by 15,000 workers at the automaker's plants in Oshawa, Ontario and Ste-Therese, Quebec.

The Canadian Auto Workers members struck at midnight Wednesday after labour contract talks between GM and the union broke down over the issue of shifting work to outside suppliers, known as outsourcing.
Another 5,700 workers at engine and components plants in St. Catharines, Ontario, are scheduled to strike just before midnight on Sunday.
The rest of GM Canada's 26,000 workers are scheduled to walk out on Oct. 9 if the automaker and union fail to reach a settlement for a new national labour pact.
Meanwhile, the United States, GM said it and United Auto Workers have not scheduled any negotiations over the weekend for a new pact covering the automaker's 215,000 U.S. hourly workers.
Charles Licari, GM's labour spokesman, said the recess in the talks was not related to the Canadian strike. It was designed to give negotiators rest, he said.
"There are no formal meetings scheduled over the weekend, but there always is some informal dialogue going on," Licari said.

UAW President Stephen Yokich has been in close contact with CAW President Buzz Hargrove throughout the talks and said Thursday it was unclear whether the UAW could reach an agreement during the Canadian strike.
The strike in Canada already is curtailing supplies of GM's popular full-size, extended-cab pickup trucks and its Chevrolet Lumina mid-size cars.
Parts plant shutdowns in Canada are expected to affect production of Cadillac luxury cars and Chevrolet Cavalier and Pontiac Sunfire small cars in the United States next week, analysts say.
In addition, an extended strike could wreak havoc on production launches of several important new GM car models that use transmissions and other parts made in Canada.

In a statement rleased Friday, Hargrove said fruitless meetings with GM amounted to a "donkey dance" but said he would be available to meet with GM bargainers over the weekend if they can meet his demands on outsourcing.
